problem: "temporal advantage" rendered "material advantage" (shifts sense from worldly/earthly to material).
replacement: We must first understand what the purpose of society and the aim of government are taken to be. Suppose you intend to raise the human mind to a certain height and to teach it to look on the things of this world with generous feelings. Suppose you want to inspire in people a scorn for mere worldly advantage, to give birth to living convictions, and to keep alive the spirit of honorable devotion. Suppose you think it good to refine a nation’s habits, to improve its manners, to cultivate its arts, and to promote the love of poetry, of beauty and of renown. Suppose you want to form a people able to act with power on all other nations, and prepared for those high enterprises that, whatever the outcome of its efforts, will leave a name famous for all time. If you believe that these are the principal objects of society, you must avoid the government of democracy, which would be a very uncertain guide to the end you have in view.

problem: Term drift: "manners of the people" (mœurs) should be "customs" under the STYLE-NOTE manners rule.
replacement: The majority supposes that its right to govern society comes from its superior intelligence. This idea was brought into the United States by the first settlers. It would be enough by itself to create a free nation, and it has now merged with the customs of the people and with the small details of social life.

problem: "fatal in itself" softened to "harmful in itself"; judgment made milder.
replacement: In the United States political questions cannot be posed in so general and absolute a way. All parties are willing to recognize the rights of the majority, because all hope to turn those rights to their own advantage at some future time. The majority in that country therefore exercises a prodigious actual authority and a moral influence that is scarcely less preponderant. No obstacles exist that can hinder its progress, or even slow it down, or make it heed the complaints of those it crushes along its path. This state of affairs is disastrous in itself and dangerous for the future.

I am therefore of the opinion that one social power must always be made to predominate over the others. But I think liberty is in danger when this power meets no obstacles that might slow its course and force it to moderate its own vehemence.

Suppose, on the other hand, that a legislative power could be constituted so as to represent the majority without necessarily being the slave of its passions. Suppose an executive could be constituted so as to keep a certain degree of uncontrolled authority, and a judiciary so as to remain independent of the other two powers. A government would then be formed that would still be democratic without any risk of tyrannical abuse.

problem: Term drift: "manners of the country" (mœurs) should be "customs".
replacement: I do not say that tyrannical abuses often occur in America today. But I maintain that no sure barrier is set against them, and that the causes that moderate the government are to be found in the circumstances and customs of the country more than in its laws.

problem: "to their vigilance" omitted in "confides the task of serving its designs to their vigilance".
replacement: In the United States the unbounded power of the majority favors the legal despotism of the legislature, and it equally favors the arbitrary authority of the magistrate. The majority has complete control over the law, both when it is made and when it is carried out. It has equal authority over those who hold power and over the community at large. It therefore regards public officials as its passive agents and readily entrusts the task of serving its designs to their vigilance. The details of their office and the privileges they are to enjoy are rarely defined in advance. Instead the majority treats them as a master treats servants who are always working under his eye, and whom he can direct or reprimand at any moment.

In America the majority raises very formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion. Within these barriers an author may write whatever he pleases, but he will regret it if he ever steps beyond them. He is not exposed to the terrors of an auto-da-fé, but he is tormented by the slights and persecutions of daily abuse. His political career is closed forever, because he has offended the only authority that can advance his success. Every kind of compensation, even that of celebrity, is refused him. Before he published his opinions, he imagined he shared them with many others. But as soon as he has declared them openly, his overbearing opponents loudly condemn him, while those who think as he does but lack the courage to say so abandon him in silence. In the end he gives way, worn down by his daily efforts, and he falls silent, as if tormented by remorse for having spoken the truth.

problem: "immaculate in their manners" (mœurs, morals) left as "manners"; reads as etiquette.
replacement: If great writers have not yet appeared in America, the reason is simply given by these facts. There can be no literary genius without freedom of opinion, and freedom of opinion does not exist in America. The Inquisition was never able to stop a vast number of anti-religious books from circulating in Spain. The empire of the majority succeeds much better in the United States, since it actually removes the wish to publish such books. There are unbelievers in America, but, to tell the truth, there is no public voice of unbelief. Some governments have tried to protect the morality of nations by banning licentious books. In the United States no one is punished for writing this sort of work, but no one is tempted to write it. This is not because all the citizens are spotless in their morals, but because the majority of the community is decent and orderly.

problem: Term drift: "felt more in manners than in the conduct of society" (mœurs) should be "customs".
replacement: The effects of the tyranny of the majority have so far been felt more in customs than in the conduct of society. They check the development of leading characters. Democratic republics organized like the United States put the practice of courting favor within the reach of the many. Proofs of this spirit in the United States. Why there is more patriotism in the people than in those who govern in its name.

problem: "speculate upon its foibles" (profit from) rendered "study its weaknesses"; sense of exploiting lost.
replacement: In free countries, everyone is more or less called on to give his opinion on affairs of state. In democratic republics, public life is constantly mixed up with domestic affairs, the sovereign authority is accessible from every side, and its attention can almost always be caught by shouting. In such countries more people are found who play on its weaknesses and live at the expense of its passions than in absolute monarchies. This is not because men are naturally worse in these States than elsewhere, but because the temptation is both stronger and easier to reach. The result is a far more widespread debasement of the character of citizens.
